title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As in every large household, at Bald Hills there existed several quite distinct worlds, which merged into one harmonious whole, though each kept its own particular character and made concessions to the others. Every event that took place in that house, joyful or sad, mattered to all these worlds, but each had its own particular reasons for rejoicing or grieving over it, independent of the others.
Pierre's return, for instance, was a joyful and important event, and every one of them felt it to be so.

The servants—the most reliable judges of their masters, since they judge not by what they say or the feelings they express but by their actions and their way of living—were glad of Pierre's return, because they knew that with him around Count Nicholas would stop going out to the estate every single day, and would be in better spirits and a better temper, and also because they would all get handsome presents at the holidays.

The children and their governesses were glad of Pierre's return because no one else drew them into the social life of the household the way he did. He alone could play, on the clavichord, that écossaise—a Scottish country dance, and his only piece—to which, as he said, every possible kind of dance could be danced, and they felt certain he had brought presents for every one of them.

Young Nicholas, now a slim, delicate, intelligent boy of fifteen, with curly light-brown hair and beautiful eyes, was thrilled, because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous, passionate devotion. No one had planted this love of Pierre in him; he saw him only now and then. Countess Mary, who had raised him, had done everything she could to make him love her husband the way she loved him, and little Nicholas did love his uncle, but with just a shade of contempt mixed in. Pierre, though, he adored. He did not want to be a hussar or a Knight of St. George like Uncle Nicholas; he wanted to be learned, and wise, and kind, like Pierre. In Pierre's presence his face always lit up with pleasure, and he would flush and go breathless whenever Pierre spoke to him. He never missed a single word Pierre said, and would afterward, with Dessalles or alone, recall and turn over in his mind the meaning of everything Pierre had said. Pierre's past life, and his unhappiness before 1812—of which young Nicholas had formed a vague, poetic picture from a few words he had overheard—his adventures in Moscow, his captivity, Platon Karataev, of whom he had heard from Pierre, his love for Natasha, of whom the boy was also especially fond, and above all Pierre's friendship with the father Nicholas could not remember—all of it made Pierre, in his eyes, a hero and a saint.

From broken remarks about Natasha and his father, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of that dead father, and from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy, only just beginning to guess what love was, had formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha, and, dying, had left her to his friend. But the father the boy could not remember appeared to him a divinity he could not picture, one he never thought of without his heart swelling and tears of sadness and rapture coming to his eyes. And so the boy, too, was happy that Pierre had arrived.
The guests welcomed Pierre because he always helped enliven and bring together whatever company he found himself in.
The grown members of the family, not to mention his wife, were glad to have back a friend whose presence made life run more smoothly and peacefully.
The old ladies were pleased with the presents he brought them, and, above all, that Natasha would now go back to being herself.
Pierre sensed the different outlooks of these various worlds, and hurried to satisfy all their expectations.

Though the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre, with the help of a list his wife had drawn up, had now bought everything—not forgetting his mother- and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material meant as a present for Belova, nor the toys for his wife's nephews. In the early days of their marriage it had struck him as strange that his wife should expect him not to forget to buy every single thing he had undertaken to buy, and he had been taken aback by her real annoyance the first time he came home from a trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew used to this expectation. Knowing that Natasha never asked anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he himself had first offered to take them on, he now found an unexpected, almost childlike pleasure in buying presents for everyone in the house, and never forgot a single one. If Natasha found fault with him now, it was only for buying too much, and things that were too expensive. To her other supposed faults—untidiness and neglect of herself, faults most people saw as such but which Pierre thought of as qualities—she had now added stinginess.

From the time Pierre began living as a family man, on a footing that meant heavy expenses, he had noticed, to his surprise, that he spent only half what he used to, and that his affairs—which had been in disorder lately, chiefly because of his first wife's debts—had begun to improve.

Life had become cheaper because it was more confined. The most expensive luxury of all is a life that can be changed at any moment—and that luxury was no longer his, nor did he want it any longer. He felt that his way of life had now been settled once and for all, until death, and that it was no longer in his power to change it. So that way of life proved economical.
With a merry, smiling face, Pierre was sorting through his purchases.
"What do you think of this?" he said, unrolling a piece of cloth like a shopkeeper.
Natasha, sitting across from him with her eldest daughter on her lap, turned her sparkling eyes swiftly from her husband to the things he was showing her.
"That's for Belova? Excellent!" She felt the quality of the material. "It was a ruble an arshin, I suppose?"
Pierre told her the price.

"Too dear!" Natasha said. "How pleased the children will be, and Mamma too! Only you needn't have bought me this," she added, unable to hold back a smile as she gazed admiringly at a gold comb set with pearls, of a kind just then coming into fashion.
"Adèle tempted me: she kept insisting I buy it," Pierre answered.
"When am I supposed to wear it?" and Natasha stuck it into her coil of hair. "When I take little Masha into society? Maybe it'll be fashionable again by then. Well, come along now."
And, gathering up the presents, they went first to the nursery, and then to the old countess's rooms.
The countess was sitting with her companion Belova, playing a game of grand-patience as usual, when Pierre and Natasha came into the drawing room with parcels under their arms.
The countess was now past sixty, entirely gray, and wore a cap with a frill framing her face. Her face had shriveled, her upper lip had sunk in, and her eyes had grown dim.

After the deaths of her son and her husband in such quick succession, she felt herself a person accidentally forgotten by the world, left with no aim or purpose for her existence. She ate, drank, slept, or lay awake, but she did not live. Life gave her no new impressions. She wanted nothing from life but peace, and only death could give her that peace. But until death came she had to go on living—that is, to keep using her vital forces. A peculiarity one notices in very small children and very old people alike was especially plain in her. Her life had no outward aims left—only a need to keep exercising her various functions and inclinations remained visible. She had to eat, sleep, think, speak, weep, work, vent her anger, and so on, simply because she had a stomach, a brain, muscles, nerves, and a liver. She did none of these things under any outward pressure, the way people in the full vigor of life do, for whom the purpose behind exercising their own functions goes unnoticed, hidden behind whatever goal they're chasing. She talked only because she had a physical need to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried the way a child cries, because her nose needed clearing, and so on. What is a goal, for people in full vigor, was for her evidently merely a pretext.
So, in the mornings—especially if she had eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and would seize on the handiest pretext: Belova's deafness.
She would begin saying something to her, in a low voice, from the far end of the room.
"It seems a little warmer today, my dear," she would murmur.
And when Belova answered, "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Good Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another pretext would be her snuff, which would seem too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew, by unfailing signs, exactly when Belova would be deaf again, the snuff damp again, and the countess's face yellow again. Just as she needed to work off her ill temper, so too she sometimes needed to exercise her still-surviving faculty of thought—and the pretext for that was a game of patience. When she needed to cry, the late count would serve as pretext. When she wanted to be agitated, Nicholas and his health would be the pretext, and when she felt the need to speak spitefully, Countess Mary would serve. When her vocal organs needed exercise, usually around seven o'clock, once she had rested after dinner in a darkened room, the pretext would be retelling the same old stories over and over to the same listeners.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it aloud, and everyone made every possible effort to see to her needs. Only in a rare glance, exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary, was their shared understanding of her condition ever expressed.

But those glances said something more besides: they said that she had already played her part in life, that what they now saw before them was not the whole of her, that we must all become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to hold themselves back for the sake of this once-precious person, once as full of life as they themselves now were, but now so much to be pitied. "Memento mori"—remember that you must die—said those glances.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid ones in that household, and the very young children failed to understand this, and steered clear of her.
